title: The War for the Human Soul: Five Lessons from C.S. Lewis's Space Trilogy
author: Simple Men
summary: This essay reads C.S. Lewis's Space Trilogy (Out of the Silent Planet, Perelandra, That Hideous Strength), written during World War II, as a prophetic map of contemporary ideological battles -- technocratic dehumanization, institutional capture disguised as 'progress,' and a direct assault on masculine virtue. Framing the argument explicitly for Christian men, the piece works through two of its five lessons in detail: that Earth itself is a contested battleground rather than a place of achievable peace, and that evil frequently disguises itself as institutional progress. The second lesson draws heavily on Lewis's fictional N.I.C.E. (National Institute of Co-ordinated Experiments) from That Hideous Strength, portrayed as a bureaucratic, well-funded institution that recruits not monsters but 'hollow men' stripped of classical formation and genuine virtue, available to be shaped by whatever institution offers them status. The author connects this directly to Lewis's own prose, quoting his description of a man whose education was 'neither scientific nor classical -- merely Modern' and who consequently lacked the moral resources to resist real threats. The piece's overall claim is that recognizing institutional evil requires a formed conscience, and that failing to recognize the spirit of the N.I.C.E. in its 'contemporary forms' leaves a man serving it without ever understanding what he's doing.
points: Lewis wrote the Space Trilogy between 1938 and 1945, and the author argues it accurately anticipated technocratic dehumanization, institutional capture disguised as progress, and an explicit assault on masculine virtue decades before those became live cultural debates.

Lesson on Earth as 'the silent planet': Lewis frames Earth as the one world cut off from cosmic harmony by the presence of evil, a reminder that discomfort and resistance are the expected condition of a fallen world, not evidence that something has gone wrong.

The novel's N.I.C.E. institution recruits not through obvious villainy but by offering status and belonging to 'hollow men' whose education was 'neither scientific nor classical -- merely Modern' and who therefore lack the moral resources to resist.

Lewis's own prose is used as direct evidence: a chilling passage has a N.I.C.E. operative explain that maintaining a fierce Left and fierce Right, each terrified of the other, is how real power stays hidden and unaccountable.

The essay's practical charge to readers: a man who cannot recognize the spirit of institutional evil in its contemporary forms -- corporations, universities, media organizations, cultural movements -- will serve it without ever knowing what he's doing.
quotes: Lewis wrote the Space Trilogy between 1938 and 1945, in the middle of WWII, and it's quite impressive how he managed to predict so accurately what our very own postmodern ideological landscape would look like.

Masterfully, Lewis reminds us that our world is a fallen one, in which fighting will always be a necessity. This is an important reminder for us, because forgetting the truth of the earth as a battleground will make us more liable to fall into nihilism, despair, or pleasure-seeking.
The lesson for us then, is that discomfort, resistance, and cultural hostility are the expected conditions of a fallen world in which we've chosen to reject God.
The N.I.C.E. is Lewis's portrait of institutional evil, as a bureaucratic, well-funded, and respectable entity that claims to seek progress, science, and the betterment of mankind.

His education had been neither scientific nor classical--merely "Modern." The severities both of abstraction and of high human tradition had passed him by: and he had neither peasant shrewdness nor aristocratic honour to help him.

Isn't it absolutely essential to keep a fierce Left and fierce Right, both on their toes and each terrified of the other? That's how we get things done. Any opposition to the NICE is represented as a Left racket in the Right papers and a Right racket in the Left papers.

A man who cannot recognize the spirit of the N.I.C.E. in its contemporary forms (corporations, universities, media organizations, cultural movements, Hollywood), is a man who will serve it without ever knowing what he's doing or understanding why it's wrong.
